summary: Every satellite starts with a Go or No-Go call. In Go/No-Go, you and your crew members will make that call yourselves. You can pick one out of four missions from watching the Earth to mapping the Moon to replaying a real NASA mission from 2009. Each has its own difficulty, from Cadet, which names every problem for you, to Director, with a tight budget and goals that pull against each other. Some numbers on the design board are blank, and the answers are hidden in clues around the rooms. Find them together, choose from 42 parts based on a real spacecraft, build each satellite by hand and launch it. Once in orbit, solar storms, failing parts, power faults, wildfires and false alarms hit your satellite, and you read the consoles, work out what happened and fix them with a short minigame. NASA data runs throughout the game, from part specifications and solar storms to Earth and Moon maps, spacecraft models,  and real mission facts. You can hear NASA recordings of real countdowns and liftoffs, music made by our own code, and your teammates talking to you live. Every choice costs mass, power, money or data. That is the trade-off real engineers face.
details:
Source code: https://github.com/TerryTanJR/Go-No-Go.git

Play the game: https://terrytanjr.github.io/Go-No-Go/

What it does and how it works

Go/No-Go puts you and your crew inside a space agency for one mission. You design a satellite, build it with your own hands, launch it, and then live with what you built. You move through two rooms in first person, the control room and the assembly bay, and can switch to a third-person view at any time.

There are four missions at three difficulty levels, plus a guided training mission and a sandbox with no budget limit.

  • Cadet: Eyes on Earth, an Earth-watching mission. A bigger budget, fewer parts, fewer blank values, a color-coded dashboard, and every event named for you.
  • Engineer: Map the Moon, which sends a satellite to lunar orbit, and Rewrite History, which replays the Orbiting Carbon Observatory from 2009. The dashboard shows only numbers, more values are hidden, and you work out what went wrong yourself, with a few minutes per turn.
  • Director: Wildfire Watch. A tight budget, goals that pull against each other, every value blank, failures that are only named, and 90 seconds per turn.

A short briefing from your flight director sets the goal, the budget, the lifetime and a limit on instruments. The design board in the control room lists 42 parts in nine categories: science instruments, batteries, solar arrays, antennas, computers, attitude control, propulsion, radiation shielding and ground stations. You also choose an orbit and a rocket from six options each.

Some part values are blank. The missing numbers are hidden in clues around both rooms, such as notes, books, boards and papers on the floor, and each clue is visible only to the player who zooms in on it. If a battery’s capacity is blank on the board and the note with that number is in the assembly bay, someone has to walk over, read it and call it out before anyone can check the power margin. The dashboard tracks budget, mass, power, data and communications margins as you choose, and shows “not enough data” until the blanks are filled. Designs can be saved and shared with a code.

A progress bar keeps the five steps in view: select, assemble, launch, operations and review. After the design is confirmed, the assembly bay lists the components you need. You fetch them from the shelves, put them on one of two benches, and build each part in the right order. A battery, for example, is made of cells, a battery management board, a heater and a housing. A wrong fit costs nothing, so you can learn by trying. Then you install the finished parts on the satellite and launch from the control room, watching the countdown, the climb and the moment the satellite is released into its orbit.

Once the satellite is in orbit, it is on its own, and things start to go wrong. Operations run for several turns, and each turn brings an event: solar and geomagnetic storms taken from NASA’s DONKI database, failing parts, power anomalies, a science opportunity, and wildfires, some real and some false alarms. You read the warnings on the four ops consoles, look up the symptoms in the manuals, decide what happened at the flight director desk, and then play a short minigame that matches the problem, such as balancing the power load, dodging a storm, locking an antenna onto a target, rewiring a circuit or scanning for fire. A rare surprise shows up now and then. A report at the end shows what worked, what failed and why, and compares your design with real missions.

The countdown, the pad roar and the distant rumble of the launch come from NASA recordings of real launches, and the quiet radio waves in the operations room come from a NASA recording of the Juno spacecraft. Interface sounds and the background music are generated by our own code.

You can play alone, or in a room of two to four players using a room code. In a team, Assembly and Control are different jobs: only Control sees the dashboard and only Assembly touches the parts. Teammates talk in live voice chat, with mic mute and a volume control, so the two sides really have to talk to each other. Before the mission starts, everyone presses ready in a lobby, the team picks a name and a logo, and each player builds their own astronaut with a suit, a helmet, a visor and gear.

Benefits and impact

Players feel why spacecraft design is a set of trade-offs. Every choice costs mass, power, money or data, and a bad choice can end in a failed launch. They also see real numbers, so a camera, a battery or a radio has a believable size and cost. Every value in the game data has a source entry that says whether it is sourced, derived or estimated, so a teacher can check any number. The interface is in English and Traditional Chinese, and the game runs offline on an ordinary laptop.

We want students and curious people to understand how a space mission is decided. Engineers rarely get everything they want, so they trade one thing for another and then make a Go or No-Go call. The game is meant to be played in one session in a classroom or club, and it points players to the NASA resources behind each number.

Tools and technology

Unity 6000.6.8f1 and C#. The simulation lives in its own assembly with a unit test project that covers scoring, balance, launch timing, minigames, sessions and data. Unity packages used are Universal Render Pipeline, Cinemachine, Input System, Splines, Timeline, glTFast and Draco for importing NASA models, Netcode for GameObjects, Unity Multiplayer Services, Unity Vivox and Newtonsoft Json. Python scripts with Pillow and numpy fetch NASA DONKI events and process textures and audio. Blender was used for the facility rooms, the launch complex, the avatar parts and the smoke effect. Fonts are Noto Sans TC, Rajdhani, Share Tech Mono and JetBrains Mono. The game runs on an ordinary laptop with no special hardware.

What makes it creative

We turned a systems engineering process into something you walk through instead of a table you read. You find the numbers yourself, trade them against each other, and then watch what happens in orbit. Parts are built by hand from their real subcomponents, so you learn what is inside a battery or a radio before you trade it off. And the Rewrite History mission lets players compare their design with what NASA actually flew.

What we considered

Data limits. The DONKI events are a saved snapshot of 14 notable events, so the game works offline. It does not call DONKI live while you play. Some assembly component lists are simplified teaching content, not real specifications, and the game data says so. Two events for the 2009 mission were added by hand because that period had no big storms.
Accessibility. A training mission, hints for Cadet players, three difficulty levels, larger text, English and Traditional Chinese, and no special hardware.
Cost and licensing. We used NASA media under NASA media usage guidelines with credit, open fonts, and no NASA logo. The title screen says this is a fan-made educational game with no NASA endorsement.
Scalability. Missions, parts, scenarios and events are all data files, so new content can be added without changing code.

Use of AI

The ideas, the game design and the teaching goals are our own. Most of the code, the game data files, our helper scripts and the documentation were written with Claude, an AI coding assistant from Anthropic, following our design and our feedback from playtesting. Some Blender models and scripts were also made with Claude working through Blender. The background music is not made by an AI audio model. It is generated by our own code. The flight director’s spoken briefing lines are AI generated with ElevenLabs text to speech, using a stock voice from its Voice Library and our own script. No real person’s voice is cloned.
